verdicts.trueWording: backdrop that was essentially 90 percent familiar
verdicts.note: Reactor page, raw HTML fetched (200, 83KB) and stripped: 'it was being contrasted against a backdrop that was essentially 90 percent familiar' — verbatim. Every-day-ritual limb verbatim too: 'He alters the familiar through all aspects of life, down to arbitrary everyday rituals, including myths and legends and superstitions, such as the extremely powerful lore of the riselka in Tigana.' Informs-the-whole limb: 'Each change not only alters the world... but also informs the world... until it can only be viewed as a whole, without separate parts.' Framing note (not an unsupported limb): the 90% figure is stated as the worldbuilding lesson Palmatier drew from Tigana, applied to Kay's method throughout the essay, rather than as a numeric measurement of Kay's worlds.

verdicts.trueWording: His writing is evocative, even impressionistic in places
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'Most writers... talk of his deft and lyrical skill with language. His writing is evocative, even impressionistic in places, and certainly transports one to a different world with simple word choices and turns of phrase.' Quote and both remaining limbs (transporting; simple word choices and turns of phrase) verbatim.

LitStack raw HTML fetched (200, 66KB): 'Kay relies heavily on prolepsis which is a technique where the narrator subtly reveals future outcomes first'; countdown limb verbatim in the next paragraph: 'It turns the act of reading into a countdown, forcing you to scan every sentence for the tripwires of fate.' Byline J.S. Hood, dated 30 May, 2026, as cited.

verdicts.trueWording: the battlefield is obstructed by a veil of sunlight
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'We experience the battle through the eyes of Jeane bet Ishak. Jeane is on a hillside, and the battlefield is obstructed by a veil of sunlight that reveals not the warriors themselves, but their silhouetted lunges, advances, feints and falls, and ultimately, the death of one of them, though we don't know which.' Withheld-identity limb also supported ('The last pages of the book unravel these mysteries'), and the article elsewhere calls it 'the novel's legendary final duel'. Spelling note only: the article spells the physician 'Jeane', the claim uses the novel's 'Jehane'; same character, no limb affected.

verdicts.trueWording: The novel’s momentum is driven by subtleties
verdicts.note: Raw page, section 'Subtlety that Elicits Deep Emotion': quote verbatim including the curly apostrophe, and the three exemplars follow verbatim: 'a shared look across a courtyard, a line of poetry delivered with double meaning, a slight change in a warrior's stance'.

verdicts.trueWording: could not stop finding bothersome sentence structures similar to those in The Lord of the Rings
verdicts.note: Wikipedia wikitext (action=raw, 200): 'Hobbs also stated that Kay's prose is an obstacle, because he describes a character as unconventional instead of placing that character in an action... that demonstrates the trait. He said that he could not "stop finding bothersome sentence structures similar to those in The Lord of the Rings and other contemporary fantasy novels."' Attribution to Hobbs, The Globe and Mail, confirmed in the citation. Minor page inconsistency: body says 'David A. Hobbs', the ref says first=David B.

verdicts.trueWording: use of the supernatural is described as intentionally restrained
verdicts.note: Wikipedia raw: 'Kay's use of the supernatural is described as intentionally restrained,<ref name="Wolfe-Locus"/> and the story has a "light touch with the fantasy".<ref name="Kirkus"/>' Quote verbatim; the Wolfe (Locus) and Kirkus attributions are exactly as the claim assigns them.

verdicts.trueWording: scaling down epic events so that history becomes humanized
verdicts.note: Wikipedia raw: 'Bill Capossere... also stated that the story shifts seamlessly from the macro to the micro by "scaling down epic events so that history becomes humanized".' Quote verbatim; both limbs (seamless macro-to-micro shift; humanized history) present.

verdicts.trueWording: joy of his novels is invariably in the journeys
verdicts.note: Wikipedia raw: 'The pace of the novel is generally slow, also typical of Kay's works, and in his review Alexander states that Kay is not the "sort of author to race towards a destination" and that the "joy of his novels is invariably in the journeys".' Quote verbatim; the slow-pace-is-typical limb sits inside the same Alexander-cited sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: that sometimes gets carried away with itself
verdicts.note: A Brightness Long Ago wikitext (action=raw, 200): 'A review by Kirkus Reviews stated that the book exhibits Kay's "usual elements", including numerous characters, extensive worldbuilding based on historical research, significant events altering the world, and writing "that sometimes gets carried away with itself".' Both limbs (Kirkus; among the usual elements) verbatim.

A Brightness Long Ago wikitext: 'Niall Alexander, in his review for Tor.com, states that the fringe characters were created with a "depth and tenderness and intelligence" by which the insignificant are given significance.' Quote and the insignificance limb verbatim.

The Sarantine Mosaic wikitext (action=raw, 200), Reception: Charles de Lint, reviewing Lord of Emperors — 'History aficionados will delight in all the small and telling insights Kay brings to the era and its cultures, while other readers will simply delight in the grand sweep of the story, the rich characterization, and Kay's sheer gift with language.' Both limbs verbatim; the only difference from the claim's quote is the apostrophe glyph (page uses a straight apostrophe, the claim a curly one).

Under Heaven (novel) wikitext (action=raw, 200): 'Michael Dirda, in his review for The Washington Post, Beware Gift Horses, noted that Kay has leavened the story with "appealing minor characters" that enhance the richness of the plot.' Quote and the leavening limb verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: I reserve the right to change, or telescope events
verdicts.note: Under Heaven (novel) wikitext quote box, sourced to 'Under Heaven's Author's letter by Guy Gavriel Kay at Brightweavings': 'if I base a book on a slightly altered past the reader who knows what happened in that time and place does not know with any certainty what will happen in my story. In Under Heaven I've served notice with the shift to an imagined Kitai from real China that I reserve the right to change, or telescope events.' Quote verbatim; the history-knowing-reader-cannot-predict limb is the preceding sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: in-depth examination of so many characters slows the tale down
verdicts.note: The Last Light of the Sun wikitext (action=raw, 200): 'In a review for Quill & Quire, Cori Dusmann stated that the "in-depth examination of so many characters slows the tale down" with "every question answered ... and little left to wonder about".' Quote verbatim; both the Dusmann attribution and the little-left-to-wonder limb present.
